steps.title: Interactive: Room-by-Room Safety Checklist
steps.content:
Use this checklist during every visit to reduce falls and injuries.

LIVING AREAS
- Clear clutter and secure cords along walls.
- Remove or tape down loose rugs.
- Ensure lamps and light switches are easy to reach.
- Keep frequently used items within reach.

BATHROOM
- Check that grab bars are sturdy.
- Use non-slip mats in tub and on floor.
- Set water heater below 120°F to avoid burns.
- Never rush a client who needs help toileting or bathing.

BEDROOM
- Keep a nightlight on.
- Place a lamp and phone within reach of the bed.
- Ensure the path from bed to bathroom is clear.

KITCHEN
- Clean spills immediately.
- Keep heavy items at waist level.
- Never leave cooking unattended.
- Check that smoke detectors work.

OUTDOORS / ENTRY
- Remove leaves, ice, or objects from walkways.
- Ensure handrails are secure.
- Lock doors and set alarms per the care plan.

steps.title: Body Mechanics & Safe Lifting
steps.content:
PROTECTING YOUR BACK
Caregiving often requires bending, lifting, and assisting with movement. Using proper body mechanics protects you and the client from injury.

LIFTING RULES
- Plan the lift before you begin.
- Keep your feet shoulder-width apart for a stable base.
- Bend your knees and keep your back straight.
- Lift with your leg muscles, not your back.
- Hold the load close to your body.
- Avoid twisting; turn your whole body.
- Do not reach or jerk.

TRANSFERS
- Explain each step to the client.
- Use a gait or transfer belt when available and you are trained.
- Lock wheelchair brakes before standing transfers.
- Never pull a client up by the arms or wrists.
- Ask for help when a client needs more support than you can safely provide.

WHEN TO STOP
If a client is too heavy, uncooperative, or the surface is unsafe, stop and call the office for assistance. Your safety matters too.

steps.title: Outdoor, Vehicle & Personal Safety
steps.content:
OUTDOOR SAFETY
- Scan the area before approaching the home.
- Park in well-lit, visible spots when possible.
- Have your visit bag ready and keep one arm free.
- Walk directly to the residence in a businesslike manner.
- Trust your instincts; leave and call the office if you feel unsafe.

VEHICLE SAFETY
- Keep your vehicle in good working order with enough fuel.
- Do not transport clients in your personal vehicle unless the agency and client have given written consent.
- Keep a valid driver's license and insurance if driving is required.
- Lock your car when parked or driving.
- Turn on emergency flashers and wait for police if you have car trouble.

PERSONAL SAFETY
- Wear non-slip, closed-toe shoes.
- Wear your ID badge and professional attire.
- Keep your phone charged and available for emergencies.
- Avoid carrying purses or valuables into the home.
- Report aggressive behavior, threats, animal bites, or unsafe situations to the office immediately.

steps.title: When to Call 911
steps.content:
CALL 911 IMMEDIATELY WHEN YOU SEE:
- Chest pain or pressure lasting more than a few minutes.
- Sudden severe shortness of breath.
- Uncontrolled bleeding.
- Severe burns or allergic reaction (swelling, hives, trouble breathing).
- Signs of stroke: face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty.
- Signs of heart attack: chest pain, sweating, nausea, pain in arm or jaw.
- A fall with suspected head injury, broken bone, or inability to move safely.
- A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or repeating without recovery.

WHILE WAITING FOR 911:
- Stay calm and reassure the client.
- Keep the person in a safe position.
- Do not give food or drink if choking, vomiting, or unconscious.
- Control bleeding with direct pressure using a clean cloth.
- Do not move an injured person unless immediate danger is present.

AFTER CALLING 911:
Call the office as soon as you can. Document the event, time, actions taken, and emergency responders.

steps.title: Choking & CPR Awareness
steps.content:
CHOKING
A person who cannot cough, speak, or breathe may be choking. Ask, 'Are you choking?' If they nod, call 911 and follow your training. For a responsive adult, abdominal thrusts may be used if you are trained.

CPR AND AED
CPR and AED procedures may only be performed consistent with your current training and certification. If you are not certified, focus on calling 911, keeping the airway open, and providing comfort until help arrives.

HANDS-ONLY CPR
If trained, hands-only CPR means pushing hard and fast in the center of the chest at 100 to 120 beats per minute. Do not stop until help takes over or the person responds.

RECOGNIZING CARDIAC ARREST
Signs include sudden collapse, no response, no normal breathing, and no pulse. Call 911 immediately, send someone for an AED if available, and begin CPR if trained.

STAY WITHIN YOUR SCOPE
Never perform a skill you are not trained and authorized to perform. Your role is to recognize the emergency, call for help, keep the client safe, and document.

steps.title: Interactive: 911 & Medical Emergency Guide
steps.content:
MAKING THE CALL
When you call 911, stay calm. Give the address clearly, describe the problem, and answer the dispatcher's questions. Do not hang up until told to do so.

INFORMATION TO PROVIDE
- Your exact location, including apartment number or gate code.
- The client's condition and what happened.
- Any known medical conditions or medications.
- Whether the client is conscious and breathing.

GATHERING INFORMATION
Have the client's emergency contact list, medication list, and advance directives available if possible.

STAYING SAFE
If the scene is unsafe, do not enter. Wait for emergency responders in a safe location and guide them when they arrive.

NOTIFYING THE OFFICE
After calling 911, notify your supervisor or the on-call line as soon as it is safe to do so. Follow the care plan for emergency contacts.

steps.title: Interactive: Build a Disaster Kit
steps.content:
A 3-DAY DISASTER KIT SHOULD INCLUDE:

- Water: 1 gallon per person per day.
- Non-perishable food and a manual can opener.
- First aid kit and prescription medications.
- Flashlight, battery-powered radio, and extra batteries.
- Phone charger and a list of emergency contacts.
- Change of clothes and sanitation supplies.
- Copies of important documents in a waterproof bag.
- Cash and change.
- Pet supplies if applicable.

SPECIAL NEEDS
- Extra glasses, hearing-aid batteries, and mobility aids.
- Medical equipment such as oxygen or CPAP backup plans.
- Items that calm the client, such as familiar objects or comfort items.

steps.title: Scenario: Missing Client or Power Outage
steps.content:
MISSING CLIENT
- Check the home calmly, including bathrooms, backyard, and garage.
- Ask neighbors if they saw the client.
- Call the office and emergency contacts immediately.
- If the client is at risk or has been missing more than a few minutes, call 911.

POWER OUTAGE
- Use flashlights; avoid candles because of fire risk.
- Keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed.
- Follow the care plan for medical equipment that needs power.
- Report the outage and any medical needs to the office.

SEVERE WEATHER
- Stay indoors and away from windows.
- Have the client put on sturdy shoes in case evacuation is needed.
- Keep the emergency kit ready and listen to weather alerts.

steps.content: https://www.youtube.com/embed/BaHTZdJWYVw
steps.caption: CDC guidance on proper hand-washing and sanitizer use to prevent infections.

steps.title: Interactive: Hand-Washing Steps
steps.content:
WHEN TO WASH HANDS
- Before putting on gloves and after removing them.
- Before and after touching a client.
- After toileting or changing incontinence products.
- After touching contaminated surfaces, laundry, or trash.
- Before food preparation and eating.

SOAP AND WATER STEPS (20 SECONDS)
1. Wet hands with clean, running water.
2. Apply soap and lather the backs of hands, between fingers, and under nails.
3. Scrub for at least 20 seconds (sing Happy Birthday twice).
4. Rinse under clean, running water.
5. Dry with a clean towel or air dryer.
6. Use the towel to turn off the faucet if possible.

ALCOHOL-BASED HAND RUB
- Use when hands are not visibly soiled.
- Apply enough product to cover all hand surfaces.
- Rub until dry, about 20 seconds.

steps.title: Interactive: PPE & Exposure Response
steps.content:
PUTTING ON PPE (DONNING)
1. Perform hand hygiene.
2. Put on gown, if needed, opening at the back and tying securely.
3. Put on mask or respirator; mold the nose piece and secure straps.
4. Put on eye protection if splashes are possible.
5. Put on gloves last, extending over gown cuffs.

TAKING OFF PPE (DOFFING)
1. Remove gloves first, turning them inside out.
2. Remove gown by untying and rolling away from you.
3. Remove eye protection and mask.
4. Perform hand hygiene immediately.

EXPOSURE RESPONSE
- Needlestick or blood exposure: wash or flush the area immediately and report to the office.
- Seek medical evaluation promptly.
- Hepatitis B vaccine is offered to staff at risk of blood exposure.
- TB screening is required upon hire and reviewed annually.

LAUNDRY & KITCHEN
- Handle soiled laundry carefully; do not shake.
- Bag waste securely and follow local biohazard rules.
- Keep food prep areas clean and separate raw and cooked foods.

steps.title: TB & Bloodborne Pathogens
steps.content:
BLOODBORNE PATHOGENS
Bloodborne pathogens are infectious microorganisms in human blood that can cause disease. The most common are Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), Hepatitis C Virus (HCV), and HIV.

MODES OF TRANSMISSION
- Direct contact of blood or body fluids with broken skin or mucous membranes.
- Indirect contact through contaminated surfaces or objects.
- Needlestick or sharp injuries.
They are NOT spread by casual contact, hugging, coughing, or sharing toilets.

PREVENTION
- Treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious.
- Use gloves and appropriate PPE.
- Never recap needles; dispose of sharps in approved containers.
- Clean and disinfect contaminated surfaces immediately.

TUBERCULOSIS
TB is a bacterial infection that usually affects the lungs. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Screening is required upon hire and reviewed annually.

IF EXPOSED
Wash the area with soap and water, flush splashes, notify your supervisor, complete an incident report, and seek medical evaluation promptly.

steps.title: Respiratory Illness & Exposure Control
steps.content:
RESPIRATORY HYGIENE
Coughs and sneezes spread germs. Cover your mouth and nose with a tissue or elbow, dispose of tissues promptly, and perform hand hygiene.

WHEN A CLIENT HAS FLU OR COVID SYMPTOMS
- Put on a mask and gloves before close contact.
- Encourage rest and fluids.
- Monitor temperature and symptoms.
- Call the office and the client's physician for guidance.
- Wash hands often and clean high-touch surfaces.

WHEN TO SEEK URGENT CARE
- Difficulty breathing or chest pain.
- Confusion or sudden dizziness.
- Persistent high fever.
- Signs of dehydration such as very dark urine, dry mouth, or no urination for 8 or more hours.

PROTECTING YOURSELF
Stay home if you are sick and report it to the office. Get an annual flu vaccine when available and keep your immunizations up to date.

steps.title: Scenario-Based Decision Making
steps.content:
Scenario-based training helps you apply what you have learned to real situations. Read each scenario, identify the priorities, and choose the safest action.

FALL SCENARIO
You find a client on the floor. The client is alert but complains of hip pain. Do not move the client. Call 911, keep them warm and comfortable, and notify the office.

CHOKING SCENARIO
A client suddenly cannot speak and is clutching their throat while eating. Ask if they are choking. If they nod, call 911 and follow your choking-response training.

FIRE SCENARIO
You smell smoke in the client's home. Sound the alarm, help the client leave immediately, stay low under smoke, call 911 from outside, and do not re-enter.

INFECTION EXPOSURE SCENARIO
You accidentally stick your finger with a used lancet while helping a client. Wash the area immediately, notify your supervisor, complete an incident report, and seek medical evaluation.

MISSING CLIENT SCENARIO
A client with dementia is not in the home when you arrive. Search the home and yard, ask neighbors, call the office and emergency contacts, and call 911 if they are not found quickly.
